source_text: Confer nunc non spiritales catholicae fidei uiros. in quibus quantum in hac uita animus potest, cernit substantiam naturamque diuinam nullis locorum spatiis tendi, nullis liniamentorum dimensionibus figurari, sed confer carnales et paruulos nostros, qui solent auditis in allegoria membris quibusdam corporis nostri — uelut cum dicuntur oculi dei et aures dei, solent deum sibi libertate phantasmatis corporis humani specie figurare —: hos confer iam illis Manichaeis, qui solent istas nugas intentis et curiosis hominibus quasi magna secreta describere, et considera. qui tolerabilius et honestius de deo sentiant: utrum ii, qui eum forma humana summa dignitate in suo genere praedita cogitant, an ii. qui eum infinita mole diffusum, non tamen undique, sed tribus quadris infinitum atque condensum, ex una uero fissum. patentem. hiantem, laxum superius inanitate. cuneatum inferius terra tenebrarum, uel, si ita melius est dicere, apertum superius natura propria. intratum inferius aliena. ecce, ego tecum derideo carnales homines. qui nondum possunt spiritalia cogitare humana forma deum existimantes; deride et tu mecum, si potes, eos, qui tam deformem turpemque fissuram uel scissuram dei, tam inaniter supra hiulcam, tam inhoneste infra obturatam multum miserabili cogitatione imaginantur, cum hoc etiam intersit, quod isti carnales, qui humana forma deum cogitant. si ecclesiae catholicae gremio contenti cum lacte nutriendi sunt. non se in temerarias opiniones praecipitent. sed ibi studium pium quaerendi nutriant, ibi petant, ut accipiant, ibi pulsent, ut eis aperiatur, incipiunt spiritaliter allegorias parabolasque scripturarum intellegere et paulatim sapere diuinas potentias congruenter alibi aurium, alibi oculorum, alibi manuum uel pedum uel etiam alarum atque pennarum, scuti quoque et gladii et galeae ceterarumque talium innumerabilium rerum nomine enuntiari. qua intellegentia quanto magis proficiunt, tanto magis catholici esse firmantur; Manichaei uero quando figurae illius imaginationem reliquerint, Manichaei esse non poterunt. hoc enim quasi proprium atque praecelsum auctoris sui laudibus tribuunt, quod dicunt illa. quae ab antiquis figurate in libris diuina mysteria posita sunt. huic, qui ultimus uenturus erat, soluenda et demonstranda esse seruata, et propterea post istum iam neminem doctorem diuinitus esse uenturum, quia nihil iste per figuras et allegorias dixerit, cum et antiquorum, quae talia fuerant, aperiret et sua enodate manifesteque monstraret. non habent ergo isti, ad quas interpretationes reuertantur, cum illis de auctore suo legitur: iuxta unam uero partem ac latus inlustris illius ac sanctae terrae erat tenebrarum terra. quocumque se uerterint, necesse est, ut phantasmatum suorum miseria coartati in scissuras aut abruptas praecisiones et iuncturas. aut fulturas turpissimas incidant: quas non dicam de incommutabili natura dei, sed de omni natura incorporea quamuis mutabili, sicut est anima. miserrimum est credere. et tamen, si non possem me intendere ad superiora neque cogitationes meas a falsis imaginationibus. quas per sensus corporeos memoria fixas gero, in libertatem ac sinceritatem naturae spiritalis euoluere. quanto melius humani corporis forma deum cogitarem, quam illum nigrum cuneum scissurae inferiori eius adfigerem superioremque uastissimam laxitatem non inueniens. unde oppilarem, sic inmensa inanitate patentem et hiantem relinquerem ? quid ista opinione foedius ? quid tenebrosius hoc errore dici aut fingi potest ?
thought_title: Comparing Catholic and Manichaean ways of imagining God
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, contrasting how unspiritual Catholics and Manichaeans each picture God, and arguing that even the crude Catholic imagination is more honorable than the Manichaean image of a split and penetrated divine mass.
pass_a_gloss: Compare now not the spiritual men of the Catholic faith, in whom, as much as the mind can in this life, it discerns that the divine substance and nature is stretched out by no spaces of places, is shaped by no dimensions of lineaments, but compare our carnal and little ones, who are accustomed, when certain members of our body are heard in allegory, as when the eyes of God and the ears of God are said, they are accustomed to shape God for themselves by the freedom of fantasy in the form of a human body: compare these now with those Manichaeans, who are accustomed to describe those trifles to attentive and curious men as if great secrets, and consider who think more tolerably and more honorably about God: whether those who think him endowed with human form with the highest dignity in its kind, or those who think him spread out with infinite mass, yet not on every side, but infinite and dense in three squares, but from one side split, open, gaping, loose above with emptiness, wedged below by the land of darkness, or, if it is better to say it thus, open above by his own nature, entered below by another's. Behold, I with you laugh at carnal men, who are not yet able to think spiritual things, thinking God to be in human form; laugh also you with me, if you can, at those who imagine so deformed and foul a split or tearing of God, so emptily gaping above, so dishonorably stopped up below, with a very wretched thought, since this also makes a difference, that those carnal ones, who think God in human form, if they are content in the bosom of the Catholic Church, are to be nourished with milk, let them not rush themselves into rash opinions, but let them nourish there a pious zeal of seeking, there let them ask, that they may receive, there let them knock, that it may be opened to them, they begin to understand spiritually the allegories and parables of the scriptures and gradually to know that the divine powers are fittingly expressed sometimes by the name of ears, sometimes of eyes, sometimes of hands or feet or even of wings and feathers, also of shield and sword and helmet and of countless other such things; by which understanding the more they advance, the more they are strengthened as Catholics; but the Manichaeans, when they have abandoned the imagination of that figure, will not be able to be Manichaeans. For they attribute this as if the proper and most exalted thing to the praises of their founder, that they say those things which were placed figuratively by the ancients in books as divine mysteries were reserved for this one, who was to come last, to be solved and shown, and that for this reason after him no teacher was to come from God, because he said nothing through figures and allegories, since he both opened the things of the ancients which had been such and showed his own things unknotted and clearly. Therefore they do not have interpretations to which they may return, when it is read to them from their founder: but along one part and side of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness. Wherever they turn themselves, it is necessary that, constrained by the misery of their fantasies, they fall into splits or abrupt cuttings and joinings, or most foul props: which it is most wretched to believe not about the unchangeable nature of God, but about every incorporeal nature although changeable, as is the soul. And yet, if I could not direct myself to higher things nor unfold my thoughts from false imaginations, which I carry fixed in memory through bodily senses, into the freedom and sincerity of spiritual nature, how much better would I think God in the form of a human body, than attach that black wedge to the split of his lower part and, not finding with what I might stop up the upper and most vast looseness, leave it open and gaping with immense emptiness? What is fouler than this opinion? What darker than this error can be said or imagined?

choices.english: not the spiritual men of the Catholic faith
choices.why: Keeps the negative scope clear: Augustine is setting aside the spiritual Catholics to focus on the carnal ones.
rejected: the unspiritual men of the Catholic faith

choices.why: Preserves the affectionate possessive 'our' and the double description of immature believers.
Renders the ablative of means literally, keeping 'fantasy' as the glossary term for phantasma.

choices.english: infinite and dense in three squares
choices.why: Literal rendering of the spatial image Mani's myth implies; 'quadris' is kept as 'squares' to preserve the geometric oddity.
rejected: infinite and compact on three sides

choices.english: wedged below by the land of darkness
choices.why: Keeps the passive participle force and the instrumental sense of the ablative, matching the glossary term 'land of darkness.'
rejected: wedged below with the land of darkness

choices.why: Preserves the parallel with 'apertum superius natura propria' and the elliptical 'aliena' referring to another nature.
rejected: penetrated below by a foreign nature

pass_b_english: Now compare not the spiritual men of the Catholic faith—in whom, as far as the mind can in this life, it discerns that the divine substance and nature is stretched out through no spaces of place and shaped by no dimensions of outline—but compare our carnal and little ones, who, when they hear certain members of our body spoken of in allegory—as when the eyes of God and the ears of God are mentioned—are accustomed to picture God to themselves by the freedom of fantasy in the form of a human body. Compare these with those Manichaeans who are accustomed to describe these trifles to attentive and curious men as if they were great secrets, and consider. Which of them think more tolerably and honorably about God: those who think of him in human form, endowed with the highest dignity in its kind, or those who think of him spread out in an infinite mass—yet not on every side, but infinite and dense on three sides, and on one side split, open, gaping, loose above with emptiness, wedged below by the land of darkness—or, if it is better to say it this way, open above by his own nature, entered below by an alien nature? See, I join you in mocking carnal men who cannot yet think spiritual things and suppose God to be in human form. Mock with me, if you can, those who imagine so deformed and foul a split or tear in God, so emptily gaping above, so dishonorably plugged below, in most wretched thought. For this difference also exists: those carnal ones who think of God in human form, if they remain content in the bosom of the Catholic Church and are to be nourished with milk, do not hurl themselves into rash opinions, but nourish there a devout zeal for seeking, there ask that they may receive, there knock that it may be opened to them (Matthew 7:7), and they begin to understand spiritually the allegories and parables of the Scriptures and gradually to perceive that the divine powers are fittingly expressed sometimes by the name of ears, sometimes of eyes, sometimes of hands or feet or even of wings and feathers, and also of shield and sword and helmet and countless other such things. The more they advance in this understanding, the more firmly Catholic they become. But the Manichaeans, when they have abandoned the imagination of that shape, will not be able to be Manichaeans. For they attribute this as the peculiar and preeminent praise of their founder: they say that those divine mysteries which were placed figuratively in the books of the ancients were reserved for this one who was to come last, to be unlocked and demonstrated, and that for this reason no teacher would come from God after him, because he said nothing through figures and allegories, since he both opened the things of the ancients that were of that kind and displayed his own things clearly and without knots. Therefore these men have no interpretations to which they can return when it is read to them from their own founder: 'Along one part and side of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness.' Wherever they turn, constrained by the misery of their fantasies, they must fall into splits or abrupt cuttings and joinings or most shameful props—things which it is most wretched to believe, I will not say of the unchangeable nature of God, but of any incorporeal nature, however changeable, such as the soul. And yet, if I could not raise myself to higher things nor unfold my thoughts from the false imaginations which I carry fixed in memory through the bodily senses into the freedom and purity of spiritual nature, how much better would I think of God in the form of a human body than fasten that black wedge to the lower split of him and, finding nothing with which to plug the vast upper looseness, leave it gaping and open with immense emptiness? What is more foul than this opinion? What more dark than this error can be said or imagined?

problems.why: Ablative of manner, not genitive; 'multum' intensifies 'miserabili,' meaning 'in most wretched thought,' not 'their most wretched thought.'
problems.fix: in most wretched thought / with most wretched thinking

problems.why: 'quadris' here means 'sides/quarters/flanks,' not geometric 'squares.' Misleads reader about Mani's spatial myth.
problems.ruling: 'tribus quadris' means three sides/flanks; 'squares' imposes geometric precision foreign to the spatial myth.

problems.why: 'Aliena' is ablative of quality/description, not agency; 'intratum' is passive/verbal adjective meaning 'entered into,' not 'entered by.'
problems.fix: entered below by an alien nature / entered below as by another's
problems.ruling: 'intratum inferius aliena' means 'entered below by a foreign/other nature,' not 'by another's'; mistranslates the Manichaean cosmological description.

edits.old: infinite and dense in three squares
edits.new: infinite and dense on three sides
entered below by an alien nature

fixed: Changed 'in their most wretched thought' to 'in most wretched thought' to reflect the ablative of manner 'multum miserabili cogitatione'.
Changed 'in three squares' to 'on three sides' because 'tribus quadris' means 'on three sides/flanks,' not geometric squares.
Changed 'entered below by another's' to 'entered below by an alien nature' because 'aliena' is ablative of quality, not agency, and 'intratum' means 'entered into,' not 'entered by.'

last_rejected.source_quote: ibi petant, ut accipiant, ibi pulsent, ut eis aperiatur
last_rejected.why: The allusion to ask/receive, knock/open matches Matthew 7:7, but Augustine does not cite it as Scripture here; the English adds a biblical reference not in source.
last_rejected.fix: Remove '(Matthew 7:7)' or verify if Augustine intended an unmarked allusion.
last_rejected.ruling: Matthew 7:7 is a correct cross-reference for 'petant...pulsent'; adding it aids the reader without misleading.

last_rejected.quote: sometimes by the name of ears, sometimes of eyes, sometimes of hands
last_rejected.source_quote: alibi aurium, alibi oculorum, alibi manuum
last_rejected.why: English adds 'sometimes' three times; source has 'alibi' (elsewhere/at other times), not 'sometimes' repeated. Changes structure but not meaning? Actually 'alibi' means 'elsewhere/in other places,' not 'sometimes.' This is mistranslation.
last_rejected.fix: elsewhere by the name of ears, elsewhere of eyes, elsewhere of hands
last_rejected.ruling: 'alibi' rendered as 'sometimes' is within normal range for listing contexts; meaning is preserved.

last_rejected.why: 'Enodate' means 'un-knotted,' i.e., clearly, plainly; 'without knots' is awkward and obscure. The point is clear, open exposition, not literally lacking knots.
last_rejected.ruling: 'enodate' literally means 'without knots'; rendering is defensible and not a meaning change.
